chapters.title: Prologue: Poltergeist
chapters.summary:
Michael Lewis reflects on writing Liar's Poker in 1989 as a warning: he believed Wall Street's casino—where 24-year-olds like him at Salomon Brothers were paid fortunes to dispense advice they didn't understand—was unsustainable and would be exposed. Instead, readers treated the book as a how-to guide, and the excess he thought was a period piece of the 1980s intensified for two more decades.

He recalls Howie Rubin, the Salomon mortgage trader who lost $250 million at Merrill Lynch and became a scandal, then contrasts it with another mortgage trader named Howie who lost $9 billion on a single trade inside Morgan Stanley around 2007 and remained essentially anonymous. The mortgage bond machine born on Salomon's trading floor would culminate in the worst financial disaster in history. This book tells the story from the perspective of the handful of outsiders who saw it coming—and bet against it.
chapters.takeaway: When absurdity compounds unnoticed for decades, look for the quiet outsiders betting the system is wrong.

chapters.title: 1 A Secret Origin Story
chapters.summary:
Michael Burry, a former Stanford neurology resident with an Asperger's-like social detachment and a gift for deep financial analysis, ran Scion Capital out of his home office in Santa Cruz. His value-investing stock picks, documented obsessively on his blog, attracted investors like Gotham Capital and white-shoe firms that had never met him personally; by 2003 he managed $600 million with returns far above the market.

In October 2004 Burry began studying subprime mortgage bonds and concluded that the loans underlying them—teaser-rate adjustable mortgages to borrowers with no ability to repay—guaranteed defaults once rates reset in 2007. Discovering credit default swaps allowed him to buy insurance against bonds that wouldn't fail for years, he persuaded Goldman Sachs to sell him $100 million of protection across six bonds, then raised a dedicated fund, Scion Absolute Return Vehicle. Investors like AIG FP and Bear Stearns sold the swaps believing house prices could never fall nationally.
chapters.takeaway: Independent analysis can reveal what markets refuse to see—but you must still endure being early and alone.

chapters.title: 2 In the Land of the Blind
chapters.summary:
Mike Burry needed to buy swaps on specific BBB-rated tranches—the ones most likely to default—but Wall Street had never offered such granular instruments, so Goldman Sachs created custom deals for him. Meanwhile, in New York, Steve Eisman, a blunt analyst who had made his name shorting subprime originators like Household International after his first analyst job ended when he told a client to sell a company run by crooks, began digging into the same market.

With analyst Danny Moses and researcher Porter Collins at FrontPoint Partners, Eisman toured subprime lenders' operations and was stunned by the fraud: Century City brokers in California falsifying incomes, and Ameriquest's culture of fabrication. When Eisman asked why rating agencies rated these bonds triple-A, one agency employee admitted they were paid by issuers and feared losing business if they refused. The chapter ends with Eisman realizing the entire edifice—loans, ratings, and the banks packaging them—rested on assumptions no one had verified.
chapters.takeaway: Verify the underlying assets yourself; when incentives corrupt the raters, only firsthand diligence protects you.

chapters.title: 3 "How Can a Guy Who Can't Speak English Lie?"
chapters.summary:
Greg Lippmann, a Deutsche Bank CDS trader with a pompadour and a taste for self-promotion, becomes the market's loudest evangelist for shorting subprime—partly because Deutsche Bank itself held positions needing an exit. Lippmann pitches Steve Eisman relentlessly, even printing T-shirts reading 'I'm short your house,' though Eisman distrusts him since Lippmann profits regardless of who wins.

The chapter introduces Howie Hubler, a Morgan Stanley bond trader who, unwilling to pay swap premiums, instead sold credit default protection on AAA tranches—collecting small premiums while bearing catastrophic risk—to fund his own bet against lower-rated bonds. Lewis also explains the machinery of CDOs: Wall Street took the riskiest BBB slices, repackaged them, and had rating agencies bless most of the package as triple-A. Eisman's team realizes the market isn't just blind but structurally dishonest, with everyone from loan officers to CEOs paid to keep the machine running.
chapters.takeaway: Follow who bears real risk versus who collects fees—structured complexity often hides catastrophic exposures.

chapters.title: 4 How to Harvest a Migrant Worker
chapters.summary:
Young hedge fund manager Charlie Ledley and his partners Jamie Mai and Ben Hockett at Cornwall Capital, operating from a shed in Berkeley with $110,000, built a strategy of buying cheap options on events they believed were mispriced—from Capital One's accounting to a biotech drug trial—turning their stake into tens of millions.

Their investigation of subprime led them through a surreal landscape: they interviewed mortgage brokers who admitted lying was routine ('How can a guy who can't speak English lie?' referred to Hispanic borrowers steered into bad loans), visited rating agencies where analysts conceded they couldn't scrutinize individual loans, and found that even industry insiders couldn't explain what was in the bonds. Cornwall bought CDS on the highest-yielding BBB tranches from banks eager to sell. The title reflects the predatory logic of lending: brokers harvested borrowers like crops, and no one—not regulators, not bankers, not ratings agencies—had any incentive to stop it.
chapters.takeaway: Outsiders with modest capital can exploit systemic blindness if they verify facts others won't check.

chapters.title: 5 Accidental Capitalists
chapters.summary:
Cornwall Capital formalized its bet: Charlie and Jamie were 'accidental capitalists,' having stumbled into investing after college without finance backgrounds, guided by Ben Hockett's veteran trading instincts. They attended an American Securitization Forum conference in Las Vegas in January 2007, where they watched industry insiders celebrate record subprime volumes while ignoring rising delinquencies.

Lewis details how the big shorters—Burry, Eisman's FrontPoint, Cornwall, and Greg Lippmann's clients—collectively represented tiny sums against trillions in subprime exposure. The chapter also covers the mechanics that made their trades possible and strange: swap contracts requiring annual premiums of several percent, dealers like Goldman marking positions perversely, and the growing tension between the shorts and sellers like AIG FP. As delinquency data worsened, the shorts watched the bond indices barely move, learning that markets can stay irrational long after the underlying reality has broken.
chapters.takeaway: Being right is not enough—positions must survive until the market finally admits reality.

chapters.title: 6 Spider-Man at The Venetian
chapters.summary:
At the American Securitization Forum in January 2007 at The Venetian hotel in Las Vegas, the shorts confront the industry they're betting against. Greg Lippmann works the floor selling his short thesis to anyone who'll listen—his 'Spider-Man' nickname coming from his sales patter—while Eisman attends sessions where mortgage executives dismiss rising defaults as contained.

Eisman watches a presentation by Option One executives and realizes the audience of investors asks only about bonus structures, not loan quality. He meets a young bearish analyst, Tao Wang-style voices aside, and hears HSBC announce massive writedowns on US subprime. Yet the market barely reacts: the ABX index dips and recovers. The Vegas trip crystallizes the shorts' despair—everyone in the room either doesn't understand what they own or is paid not to care. Burry, meanwhile, fights his own investors who demand their money back precisely because his thesis hasn't yet paid off.
chapters.takeaway: Conferences reveal crowd psychology: consensus comfort amid deteriorating data is a signal, not reassurance.

chapters.title: 7 The Great Treasure Hunt
chapters.summary:
As cracks appear, the shorts hunt for exactly which bonds will collapse first—a treasure hunt through loan-level data. Steve Eisman's team hires a data firm to analyze pools behind specific CDOs, discovering concentrations in Florida, California, and Las Vegas housing with fraud-riddled originators like New Century feeding the worst collateral into CDOs.

They learn about 'synthetic' CDOs—bets stacked on bets—which multiplied exposure far beyond actual mortgages: by 2007 the CDO market dwarfed the underlying loans. They encounter Wing Chau, a CDO manager at Harding Advisory who admits he vets nothing himself, simply collecting management fees while shoveling risky bonds into deals that investors trusted blindly. Eisman walks out furious. The chapter exposes how the food chain worked: lenders made bad loans, packagers sliced them, managers rubber-stamped them, and rating agencies blessed them—all compensated upfront regardless of outcomes.
chapters.takeaway: Trace the incentive chain end-to-end; fee-collectors with no skin in outcomes create hidden fragility.

chapters.title: 8 The Long Quiet
chapters.summary:
Spring and summer 2007 test the shorts' patience. Mike Burry faces investor revolt: redemptions, lawsuits, and fury over paying millions in annual swap premiums while his positions show losses—he stops answering calls, posting only terse updates on his website, convinced conviction means enduring isolation. His fund is up hugely by year's end, yet many investors had forced him out or demanded audits before the payoff.

Cornwall's Jamie and Charlie agonize over when to cash in, watching their positions swing wildly as Bear Stearns' two subprime hedge funds implode in June 2007. The market finally breaks when rating agencies begin downgrading hundreds of bonds and the ABX indices crater. Howie Hubler's Morgan Stanley position—short AAA via sold swaps—starts bleeding billions. The quiet period teaches the central lesson: holding a correct contrarian bet through doubt, loneliness, and mark-to-market pain requires psychological fortitude beyond mere analysis.
chapters.takeaway: Correct analysis demands equal parts patience and nerve—endure the lonely stretch before vindication arrives.

chapters.title: 9 A Death of Interest
chapters.summary:
The collapse arrives. In August 2007 the market for subprime-backed securities dies completely—no buyers exist at any price, and the phrase gives the chapter its title as interest in the paper vanishes overnight. Cornwall Capital, whose $30 million in swaps now marks against billions, scrambles to monetize before counterparties renege or spreads close; Ben Hockett engineers sales of their CDS back to the very banks that sold them, capturing enormous gains.

FrontPoint, restricted by its structure, cannot fully capitalize. Howie Hubler's losses balloon to roughly $9 billion, among the largest single-trader losses ever, yet Morgan Stanley buries the story. Lewis shows the human aftermath: Burry shuts his fund to outside money, wounded by the fight; Eisman is proven spectacularly right but finds no satisfaction in the wreckage. The machines that created the boom—leverage, securitization, ratings—now accelerate the bust.
chapters.takeaway: Plan your exit as carefully as your entry—winning bets are worthless if you can't collect.

chapters.title: 10 Two Men in a Boat
chapters.summary:
Charlie and Jamie, having turned Cornwall's capital into roughly $135 million (an 80-fold return on the original stake), wrestle with what comes next. They debate whether to return money, keep trading, or institutionalize; ultimately they shrink the fund, unable to replicate the rare conditions of their great trade and wary of managing others' money without a repeatable edge.

Lewis uses their deliberations to reflect on luck versus skill: their success came from recognizing mispricing, but also from timing and fortune. Eisman continues shorting—moving on to financial stocks generally, betting on the broader banking collapse—while Burry exits public life entirely, eventually reopening a small fund under his own terms. The chapter closes the personal arcs: men who saw the crash coming discover that foresight brings wealth but not belonging; the system they bet against survives, recapitalized and largely unpunished.
chapters.takeaway: Distinguish skill from luck after a windfall, and don't manage others' money without a repeatable edge.

chapters.title: Epilogue: Everything Is Correlated
chapters.summary:
Lewis surveys what changed and what didn't. He visits the ruins: Bear Stearns gone, Lehman gone, AIG rescued by taxpayers, and Goldman Sachs paying record bonuses months after the crisis. The people responsible mostly escaped rich; the few who saw it coming remain marginal figures. He recounts returning to the subject years later, noting the reforms enacted left the core machinery—too-big-to-fail banks, government-guaranteed risk-taking—largely intact.

The title refers to the lesson of correlated bets: everything tied to US housing failed together because diversification was illusory. Lewis closes with the moral he drew from Liar's Poker all along: a financial system that rewards insiders for complexity and punishes outsiders for skepticism invites repeated catastrophe. The big short's heroes profited from the crash but could not prevent it, and the conditions that produced it were already rebuilding themselves.
chapters.takeaway: Correlation destroys apparent diversification—question what happens to all holdings together in a crisis.
